newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEK BOURSE OFFICIALS CHARGED, BROKERS SEE COVERUP.
newsitem.headline: GREEK BOURSE OFFICIALS CHARGED, BROKERS SEE COVERUP.

text.p: Greece's simmering bourse scandal blew up on Tuesday when the stockbrokers association accused the government of a cover-up and a state prosecutor laid negligence charges against unnamed stock exchange officials.
"We condemn this attempt by the government which aims at ... covering up possible ... illegal actions," the Association of Athens Stock Exchange Members (SMEHA) said in a statement.
It was the most dramatic turn of events since a prosecutor brought fraud charges against one brokerage, Delta Securities, last week. Delta's assets and accounts were frozen and offices sealed.
Delta's three top officials were charged with fraud after the firm tried to settle a 2.6 billion drachma account with the bourse clearing house with bad cheques.

Brokers seized on the scandal to demand that the settlement system be investigated, with a look at brokerages on the other side of the Delta deals, to ensure the system was not abused to manipulate prices.
The government, apparently smarting from the SMEHA charge, ordered national economy ministry inspectors on Tuesday to audit 10 Athens brokerages.
Some SMEHA members have expressed suspicion about trades in the shares in textile firms Magrizos , Mills St. George and Parnassos .
Magrizos, whose shares have been tied to the Delta scandal, said its dramatic share rise and fall over the past year may have been part of a "trading game" but denied any involvement.
"It could be a trading game took place," David Magrizos, deputy managing director of Magrizos, told Reuters.
Magrizos shares traded at 201 drachmas in September 1995 and soared to 1,365 in September 1996 before closing at 911 drachmas on November 7 when the bourse crisis struck.
Most SMEHA members agreed on Tuesday to keep up a bourse boycott and a SMEHA statement accused the government of using strong-arm tactics to try to force them to resume trade.
"The government tried today to force five selected bank brokerages to conduct transactions at the Athens stock exchange. We condemn this attempt by the government," the statement said.
It was the most defiant statement so far by SMEHA towards the government, which appoints the bourse president.
With colleagues booing and shouting insults, four bank brokerages began executing a handful of trades just before the close.
The general share index closed up 0.09 percent at 918.91 on turnover of 1.71 million drachmas. Reuters screens showed trades in four bank shares only.

A number of brokers were angered by the government effort to force trading to resume, saying it gave at least the illusion of a possible cover-up with the brokerages able to close positions which might make discovering any wrongdoing easier.
"I fear that this move may be seen by the investment public as an attempt at a cover up," said broker Costas Katsoulis at Katsoulis Securities.
Most brokers have said their refusal to trade was aimed at forcing the government to clean up the settlement system and stop any abuses in the future.
In another development, a Greek prosecutor laid charges against unnamed bourse officials for negligence in connection with the Delta fraud scandal.

Prosecutor Anastassios Kanellopoulos, who laid fraud charges against Delta last week, laid the charges against unnamed bourse officials, empowering him to summon bourse officials to testify under oath.
